lead: A chip is tested many times: on the wafer, after packaging, after soldering to a board, and as a finished product. Each level uses a different fixture, catches a different fault class, and costs more than the one before. Planning what to test where — including reaching cores inside an SoC on a small pin budget — is chip-level and system-level test.
prereq: You need: test economics from 6.1, scan from 6.4 and boundary scan from 6.5.

blocks.text: The same silicon is tested at every move from wafer to product. Each level answers a different question, so a fault that slips past one level must be caught later.

items: Wafer sort. A probe card touches every die on the wafer. It runs DC checks, scan vectors and memory march tests at low speed, records a wafer map, and bad die are not packaged.

Package test (final test). After dicing and assembly, the part runs the full vector set at speed and at hot and cold temperature. It catches bond-wire, assembly and speed failures a probe cannot measure.
Board test. After soldering, checks solder bridges, open tracks, missing or rotated components. In-circuit test and boundary scan do this work.
System test. The finished product runs its own software and must work as a product, not as a chip.

blocks.text: Cost per failure rises steeply. A fault caught at wafer sort costs one die. The same fault caught at system test costs a die, a package, a board, surrounding components, and labour.
Compare testing every die at wafer sort with packaging everything.

blocks.where: C_good is test and package cost per good die shipped (₹); N is die on the wafer; c_w is wafer-sort cost per die (₹6); N_p is die reaching packaging; c_p is packaging cost per die (₹80); N_good is good die that ship (800).

blocks.text: Wafer sort is cheap per die and packaging is expensive per die, so killing a bad die before packaging throws away only the cheap step.

items: Known-good-die (KGD). A die sold unpackaged into a multi-chip module must be proved good before bonding; one bad die loses the whole module.
Multi-site test. The tester contacts many die at once, lowering c_w but needing more tester channels.
Burn-in. Parts run for hours at raised voltage and temperature to burn out early-life failures no vector set can find.

blocks.text: An SoC is built from bought-in IP blocks: a CPU core, a memory controller, a USB block. Each has its own test set and wrapper. The chip-level problem is delivering those test sets through a pin budget smaller than the sum of core needs.

items: Wrapper. A ring of cells around the core. In test mode it isolates the core, feeds vectors and captures responses. IEEE 1500 standardises this core wrapper and its serial control.
Test access mechanism (TAM). On-chip wires carrying vectors from chip pins to wrappers. Width w bits delivers w bits per cycle.
Test scheduling. Decides which cores are tested together and in what order. Cores share the TAM only if their combined widths fit in w.
Serial control. One IEEE 1149.1 TAP port drives the wrappers; its state machine is in 6.5.

blocks.where: T_core is test time for one core in cycles; P is number of patterns; L is cycles per pattern; w is TAM width in bits given to that core.

blocks.text: Splitting a TAM never shortens total time by itself: serial testing at full width and balanced parallel testing give the same cycle count. Sharing pays when a core cannot use the full width, or when a power budget forbids testing all cores at once.
Only a few universities teach TAM partitioning in detail; in practice the wrapper and schedule are fixed by the IP vendor and test engineer together.

In-circuit test (ICT) presses a bed of nails onto every net and measures each component. It is fast and thorough, but the fixture is expensive and built for one board. A flying probe moves a few needles over the board: no fixture, slower, good for prototypes.

Boundary scan replaces most nails. In interconnect test, a cell on one chip drives a track and a cell on another reads it, so an open or short between two pins is caught without physical access. The same four-wire port also loads chip-level tests.

System test is software driven: boot the product, run the application, exercise the interfaces. It is the only level testing the whole product, so it is the last place an escape can be caught — and the most expensive to debug.

Two practical limits shape this. Test compression packs scan vectors so a small pin count carries a huge pattern set. Pin count is money: every extra tester channel costs, so schedules fit the tester, not the reverse.

figure.caption: Each level uses a different fixture. A failure found higher up has already passed every cheaper level below it.

spec.aria: Four test levels stacked from wafer sort at the bottom to system test at the top, showing that cost per escaped failure rises as test moves later.

examples.question: A wafer holds 1000 die and 200 are defective, so 800 are good. Wafer sort costs ₹6 per die and catches 90 % of bad die. Packaging costs ₹80 per die. Final test, identical in both plans, catches escapes. Find cost per good die shipped (i) without wafer sort and (ii) with wafer sort, counting only wafer-sort and packaging cost.
steps: Without wafer sort: all 1000 die are packaged. Cost = 1000 × ₹80 = ₹80,000. Good die shipped = 800. Cost per good die = 80,000 ÷ 800 = ₹100.
With wafer sort: wafer test cost = 1000 × ₹6 = ₹6,000.
Bad die caught = 0.90 × 200 = 180. Die reaching packaging = 1000 − 180 = 820.
Bad die escaping to final test = 200 − 180 = 20; final test removes them, so good die shipped is still 800.
Saving = ₹100 − ₹89.50 = ₹10.50 per good die, which is 10.5 %.
examples.answer: ₹100.00 without wafer sort and ₹89.50 with it, a saving of ₹10.50 (10.5 %) per good die.
examples.check:
n_die = 1000
bad = 200
good = n_die - bad
c_wafer = 6
c_pack = 80
catch = 0.90
without = n_die * c_pack / good
caught = catch * bad
packaged = n_die - caught
with_ws = (n_die * c_wafer + packaged * c_pack) / good
print(without)
print(with_ws)
print(without - with_ws)

examples.question: An SoC has one core whose test set is 4000 patterns and 200 cycles per pattern. The chip TAM is 8 bits wide. Find the core's test time in cycles with the full TAM, and when it shares the TAM equally with a second core of the same size.
steps: Shared equally (w = 4 each): T = 800,000 ÷ 4 = 200,000 cycles for each core.

Run in parallel, the two cores take 200,000 cycles; run one after the other at full width they take 100,000 + 100,000 = 200,000 cycles. Total is the same, so sharing never shortens total time by itself. Sharing pays only when a core cannot use full width — fewer internal scan chains waste extra TAM bits — or when a power budget forbids testing all cores at once.
examples.answer: 100,000 cycles with the full 8-bit TAM and 200,000 cycles per core when the TAM is split 4 and 4 — the same total time either way for these two equal cores.
examples.check:
P = 4000
L = 200
print(P * L / 8)
print(P * L / 4)

traps: Comparing test cost per die instead of cost per good die shipped. The correct denominator is good parts leaving the line.
Forgetting that one die is tested at several levels, so total test cost is the sum over all levels.
Assuming wafer sort replaces final test. Package faults and speed failures only appear after assembly.
Mixing up scan (chip-level DFT) with boundary scan (board-level interconnect). They use different hardware and catch different faults.
Treating tester pins or TAM width as free. Every channel costs money and every wire costs area, so schedules fit a fixed budget.

quiz.q: Name the four test levels a chip passes through, in order.
quiz.a: Wafer sort, package (final) test, board test, system test.

quiz.q: Why does adding a wafer-sort step reduce cost per good die?
quiz.a: Wafer sort is cheap per die (₹6) and packaging is expensive (₹80). Removing a bad die before packaging saves the package cost.

quiz.q: A wafer has 2000 die and 300 are defective. Wafer sort costs ₹5 per die and catches 80 % of bad die; packaging costs ₹100 per die. Find cost per good die with and without wafer sort.
Why must a test schedule be built when several cores share one TAM?
quiz.a: TAM width is fixed, so widths given to cores tested at the same moment cannot exceed it. The scheduler groups cores whose widths fit together and whose test times balance, respecting pin and power limits.

quiz.q: What does an IEEE 1500 core wrapper do?
quiz.a: It isolates the core from the rest of the chip in test mode, feeds in test vectors, captures responses, and is controlled serially so the chip needs few extra pins.

quiz.q: A chip passes wafer sort and package test but fails at board test. What fault is most likely?
quiz.a: A board-level fault: solder bridge, open track, missing or rotated component, or assembly damage. The die was proved good before packaging.

quiz.q: What is known-good-die and why is it needed?
quiz.a: A die proved good before packaging or bonding. Needed for multi-chip modules and systems-in-package, where one bad die destroys the whole module.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, test scheduling is an optimisation problem: integer programs and heuristics pack cores into a TAM of fixed width under power constraints, because testing many cores at once can overheat the die. Test compression is standard on large SoCs, trading a small on-chip decompressor for a many-fold cut in tester time. Researchers now push test into the field: in-system and on-line test, where a chip checks itself during normal operation rather than only on the tester. Search for IEEE 1500, TAM partitioning and test scheduling.
